parsed_answer.content:
Understanding the difference between wildcards with ? extends T and ? super T—famously encapsulated by Joshua Bloch's mnemonic PECS (Producer Extends, Consumer Super)—is one of the most critical milestones for mastering Java's Generics and Type System. When designing reusable and type-safe APIs, invariant generic types like List<T> can severely restrict flexibility. If you have a method that expects a List<Number>, passing a List<Integer> will cause a compile-time error because generics are invariant, not covariant. Wildcards introduce subtyping flexibility to generic parameters, allowing us to safely relax these constraints while maintaining compile-time type safety.

The ? extends T syntax establishes an upper bounded wildcard. It denotes an unknown type that is either type T or a subclass of T. Because the exact compiler-known type is unknown (it could be T, Integer, Double, etc., depending on what is passed at runtime), this makes the data structure read-only from an API perspective. You cannot safely add items other than null to a ? extends T collection because the compiler cannot guarantee that the object you are inserting matches the specific subtype present in the list at runtime. Conversely, ? super T establishes a lower bounded wildcard, denoting an unknown type that is either type T or a superclass of T (such as Object when T is Integer). This makes the collection a write-safe consumer. You can safely write instances of T (or its subclasses) into a ? super T collection because any supertype of T is guaranteed to be able to hold instances of T safely without violating type integrity.

rows: Safe: Returns items castable to T
Unsafe: Returns only Object, losing type context
Unsafe: Only null is allowed (immutability enforced)
Safe: Can accept T and all subtypes of T
Reading data out of a source structure (e.g., source collections)
Writing data into a sink structure (e.g., target collections)

bullet_list: Type Erasure Impact: At bytecode level, both ? extends T and ? super T are erased. ? extends T erases to its upper bound T (or Object if no explicit bound exists), while ? super T erases to Object. The compiler inserts synthetic checkcast instructions during reads to maintain type safety.

Capture Conversion: When the compiler encounters a wildcards-based signature, it often performs capture conversion, assigning an anonymous fresh type variable (e.g., CAP#1) to safely reason about operations within method scopes.

The Null Exception: Regardless of whether you use extends or super, the literal null can always be added to any wildcard-typed collection because null is legally assignable to any reference type in Java.

parsed_answer.content: A classic trap for senior engineers is trying to use a wildcard-parameterized collection for both reading and writing simultaneously. If your method signature uses List<? extends T>, you cannot mutate the list. If you use List<? super T>, reading from it forces you to downcast from Object. If a data structure must both consume and produce elements of type T, avoid wildcards entirely and use an invariant declaration like List<T>.

title: What is the difference between ? extends T and ? super T? (PECS)
